title: The Ego Detector
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart offers a single decision test for commitments: ask whether you would still do something if you could tell no one about it. He ties it to David Brooks's idea of the second mountain, where the aim is usefulness to others rather than self-service. His own example is a public reading challenge that turned a good habit into pressure and performance, and a second is the familiar pressure on teachers to sponsor a club for fear of what the boss or students will think. Applying the test to a Japanese Culture Club, he concludes he would decline because the cost to his classroom or home life is too high. The argument is that ego-driven yeses misalign with a person's real objectives and quietly cost the finite hours of a life, which are better spent on something bigger than oneself.
points: The secrecy test separates commitments chosen for real value from those chosen for reputation, respect or guilt avoidance.
Attaching social display to a good activity, as with the public reading challenge, can turn it into pressure and performance.
Saying no to a club sponsorship is defended as aligning with the school's core mission, which good leaders protect rather than their own image.
Time is finite and has to be spent somewhere, so ego-driven commitments crowd out the work and home life that matter most.
quotes: The next time you’re tempted to say yes to sponsoring a club, pursuing a degree, joining a committee, or reading a book, ask yourself: If I couldn’t tell a soul about this, would I still do it?

But the thing is, if I sponsor the club or read the book or get the PhD partly so that I can tell people about it or so that people will respect me or so that I won’t feel guilty — in short, if I do things in service of me — then I’m going to make decisions that poorly align with my life’s key objectives, and these decisions will pick away at my soul as they extract whatever hours of labor they cost.

I went and took a naturally good thing — reading — and I attached these artificial, ego-centered contraptions onto it, and made it something less. Reading stopped being about knowledge-building, pleasure, research, or wisdom, and it started being something about pressure and performance.

I don’t know who will sponsor the club — perhaps someone whose objective at school has something to do with the club. The junior class will persevere — surely some adult in the community will be able to guide them in their quest to plan prom.

And your boss will only think poorly of you if he or she views the purpose of school vaguely. People like you and me seek to make our bosses look good by focusing on the core mission of the school while living peaceably with the students, parents, and colleagues we work with.
I’m no creator of time. It all has to come from somewhere, and a day is coming when it’ll run out. Might as well use it on something much bigger than me.
